The subspace $I=x\mathbb C[x]$ is nonzero and proper. Multiplication by $x$ preserves $I$, $s(x^n)=(-1)^n x^n$ preserves $I$, and step 1.1 shows $y(x^n)\in I$ for every $n\ge1$: for $n=1$ it is zero, while for $n\ge2$ its polynomial degree is $n-1\ge1$. By [F3], this is the polynomial standard module; [F4] places it and its submodules in $\mathcal O_c$.

The quotient $\mathbb C[x]/I$ is one dimensional; $x$ and $y$ act by zero and $s$ acts trivially, so it is simple. If the displayed exact sequence split, its complement would be a one-dimensional submodule $J$ mapping isomorphically to the quotient. A generator $f\in J$ would have nonzero constant term; rescale so $f(0)=1$. Since $xJ\subseteq J$, there would be a scalar $\lambda$ with $xf=\lambda f$, or $(x-\lambda)f=0$. The polynomial ring $\mathbb C[x]$ is an integral domain and both factors are nonzero, a contradiction. The sequence is nonsplit, so $\mathcal O_c$ is not semisimple.

derivations.claim: Choose a basis $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ of $\mathfrak h^*$ and its dual $y_1,\ldots,y_n$. For $s\in S$, let $\lambda_s\ne1$ be the eigenvalue of $s$ on $\alpha_s\in\mathfrak h^*$; then $s\alpha_s^\vee=\lambda_s^{-1}\alpha_s^\vee$ and $s y=y+\lambda_s^{-1}\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee$. Put $\mathrm{eu}:=\sum_i x_i y_i+\frac n2-\sum_{s\in S}c_s s$. Using [F1], $[\sum_i x_i y_i,x]=x-\sum_s c_s\alpha_s^\vee(x)\alpha_s s$ and $[\sum_i x_i y_i,y]=-y+\sum_s c_s\lambda_s^{-1}\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee s$. The commutators of $-\sum_s c_s s$ with $x$ and $y$ are respectively $+\sum_s c_s\alpha_s^\vee(x)\alpha_s s$ and $-\sum_s c_s\lambda_s^{-1}\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^\vee s$. Hence $[\mathrm{eu},x]=x$ and $[\mathrm{eu},y]=-y$. Also $\mathrm{eu}$ commutes with $W$, because $\sum_i x_i y_i$ is the basis-independent contraction and $\sum_s c_s s$ is central by [F4].

On the degree-zero copy of an irreducible $W$-module $E$ in $\Delta_c(E)$, $\mathrm{eu}$ acts by the scalar $a_E$ of the central element $\frac n2-\sum_s c_s s$; Schur's lemma applies because $E$ is irreducible over $\mathbb C$. By $[\mathrm{eu},x]=x$, the degree-$d$ part of $\Delta_c(E)$ is an eigenspace of eigenvalue $a_E+d$.

For any $v\in M$, [F3] makes $U:=S(\mathfrak h)\mathbb C Wv$ finite dimensional and stable under $S(\mathfrak h)$ and $W$. The commuting nilpotent operators from a basis of $\mathfrak h$ have a nonzero common kernel in every nonzero such $U$: successively take the kernel of each basis operator, which is nonzero because that operator is nilpotent and is preserved by the remaining commuting operators. Call this common kernel $K$. It is $W$-stable. Since $\mathfrak h$ kills $K$, PBW gives $H_{1,c}K=\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]K$ as a vector space. The finite-dimensional space $K$ is locally finite under the linear operator $\frac n2-\sum_s c_s s$, and $[\mathrm{eu},x]=x$ shows every polynomial-degree piece of $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]K$ is finite dimensional and $\mathrm{eu}$-stable. Thus $\mathrm{eu}$ acts locally finitely on $H_{1,c}K$.

Induct on $\dim U$ to show that $\mathrm{eu}$ acts locally finitely on $v$. The zero-dimensional case is immediate. In the nonzero case, $K\ne0$ from step 2.2, so the image $\bar U$ of $U$ in $M/H_{1,c}K$ has smaller dimension. By induction some nonzero polynomial $p$ satisfies $p(\mathrm{eu})\bar v=0$, hence $p(\mathrm{eu})v\in H_{1,c}K$. Step 2.2 gives a nonzero polynomial $q$ with $q(\mathrm{eu})p(\mathrm{eu})v=0$, so the span of $\{\mathrm{eu}^jv:j\ge0\}$ is finite dimensional. This proves local finiteness for every $v$.

Each standard module $\Delta_c(E)$ has a unique simple head. Every proper submodule is stable under $\mathrm{eu}$ and therefore is a sum of its eigenspaces; it cannot meet the degree-zero copy of $E$, since $E$ is irreducible and generates $\Delta_c(E)$. The sum of all proper submodules still misses degree zero, so it is proper and contains every proper submodule. Its quotient has no nonzero proper submodule, hence is the unique simple head.

Choose finite generators of $M$ over $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$. By step 3.1 each generator is a finite sum of generalized $\mathrm{eu}$-eigenvectors; replace the generating list by these finitely many components, with generalized eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. The relation $[\mathrm{eu},x]=x$ shifts a generalized eigenvalue by $1$ under multiplication by $x$, so all eigenvalues of $M$ lie in $\bigcup_i(\lambda_i+\mathbb Z_{\ge0})$. For any fixed $\lambda$, only finitely many pairs $(i,d)$ satisfy $\lambda_i+d=\lambda$, and each $S^d(\mathfrak h^*)$ is finite dimensional; therefore every generalized eigenspace $M[\lambda]$ is finite dimensional.

Let $p(M)=\{m\in M:ym=0\text{ for every }y\in\mathfrak h\}$. It is $W$-stable, and $\mathrm{eu}$ acts on it as the central element $z=\frac n2-\sum_s c_s s$. Every vector of a $W$-module lies in the finite-dimensional span of its $W$-orbit; averaging a projection over finite $W$ shows each such span is semisimple. Thus every vector of $p(M)$ is a sum of $z$-eigenvectors with eigenvalues among the finitely many scalars $a_E$ for irreducible $W$-modules $E$. By step 4.1 the corresponding generalized eigenspaces $M[a_E]$ are finite dimensional, so $p(M)\subseteq\sum_E M[a_E]$ is finite dimensional. If $M\ne0$, choose an eigenvalue of minimal real part among the finite union of lower-bounded integer progressions containing the eigenvalues of $M$. A nonzero vector in its generalized eigenspace is killed by $\mathfrak h$, since each $y$ lowers the $\mathrm{eu}$-eigenvalue by one. Thus $p(M)\ne0$.

Every nonzero object $N\in\mathcal O$ contains a simple submodule. By [F5]–[F6], $N$ is Noetherian, because it is finite over $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$; the same is true of each submodule and quotient. By step 5.1, $p(N)$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional $W$-module. Every finite-dimensional $W$-module is semisimple: for a $W$-stable subspace, average any linear projection onto it over the finite group to obtain a $W$-equivariant projection, then induct on dimension. Choose an irreducible $W$-submodule $E\subseteq p(N)$ maximal among those occurring in $p(N)$ for the order $E<F$ when $a_F-a_E\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$. Frobenius reciprocity gives a nonzero map $\Delta_c(E)\to N$ whose image is $L:=H_{1,c}E$. Every irreducible constituent $F$ of $p(L)$ has Euler eigenvalue $a_F$, while $L$ is a quotient of $\Delta_c(E)$, whose eigenvalues are $a_E+d$ with $d\ge0$ by step 2.1. If $d>0$, then $F$ also occurs in $p(N)$ and contradicts maximality of $E$. If $d=0$, that eigenspace in $\Delta_c(E)$ is exactly its top copy of $E$, so the only constituent is $E$. Thus $p(L)=E$. Every nonzero submodule of $L$ has a nonzero singular vector by step 5.1; its singular space is a nonzero $W$-submodule of the irreducible $E$, so it contains $E$ and therefore equals $L$. Thus $L$ is simple. The same induction-reciprocity argument shows that any simple object is a quotient of some $\Delta_c(E)$.

Starting with $M_0=0$, if $M/M_j\ne0$, choose a simple submodule of that quotient by step 6.1 and let $M_{j+1}$ be its inverse image in $M$. This gives a strictly increasing chain of submodules. Noetherianity from step 6.1 forces the chain to stop after finitely many steps, at $M$. Its successive quotients are simple, so it is a finite composition series. This proves the Statement.

derivations.claim: By [F3], the assignments $x\mapsto m_x$, $w\mapsto w$, and $y\mapsto T_y$ respect every defining relation, so they give an algebra homomorphism into $\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})\rtimes W$. Filter $H_{1,c}$ by degree in $\mathfrak h$ with $\mathfrak h^*$ and $W$ in degree zero, and filter the target by differential order. The principal symbol of $T_y$ is $\partial_y$, so the associated-graded map is the localization $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]\rtimes W\otimes\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]\longrightarrow\mathbb C[\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}\times\mathfrak h^*]\rtimes W$, which is injective because a polynomial that vanishes after localization by the nonzero $\delta$ is zero. Therefore the original homomorphism is injective: a nonzero element of least filtration degree would have a nonzero leading symbol, contradicting injectivity of the associated-graded map.

After inverting $\delta$, every $\alpha_s$ is a unit by [F1]. Hence $\partial_y=T_y+\sum_s c_s\alpha_s(y)\alpha_s^{-1}(1-s)$ belongs to the localized image for every $y\in\mathfrak h$. The localized image contains all regular functions, $W$, and all constant coordinate derivations, which generate $\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})\rtimes W$. It is the whole target; injectivity is preserved by exact localization over $P$.

Localization is exact because it is localization over the commutative ring $P$. By [F4], $M_{\rm reg}$ is finite over $P[\delta^{-1}]$. Step 2.1 makes it a module over the differential operators on that ring. The coordinate derivations satisfy the Leibniz rule and commute, so they define an integrable connection. The crossed-product relations make this connection $W$-equivariant.

It remains to prove local freeness. At a closed point $p\in\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$ let $R=P[\delta^{-1}]_{\mathfrak m_p}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_pR$, and $N=(M_{\rm reg})_p$. Choose lifts $m_1,\dots,m_r$ of a basis of the finite-dimensional fiber $N/\mathfrak mN$. The quotient $Q=N/\sum_iRm_i$ is finite and satisfies $\mathfrak mQ=Q$. By [F5], some $a\in\mathfrak m$ has $(1-a)Q=0$; since $1-a$ is a unit in $R$, $Q=0$, so the lifts generate. If $\sum_i f_im_i=0$ is a nonzero relation, basis independence modulo $\mathfrak m$ forces every $f_i\in\mathfrak m$. Let $k$ be the least total order of vanishing of a nonzero $f_i$ at $p$. Some multi-index $\beta$ of order $k$ has $\partial^\beta f_i(p)\ne0$ for at least one $i$, because a nonzero regular germ has a nonzero Taylor coefficient. Apply the ordered sequence of connection derivations specified by $\beta$ to the relation. By the Leibniz rule, every term in which at least one derivation hits an $m_i$ leaves fewer than $k$ derivatives on its coefficient and vanishes modulo $\mathfrak m$. Reducing modulo $\mathfrak m$ therefore gives $\sum_i\partial^\beta f_i(p)\bar m_i=0$, a nontrivial relation among the fiber basis. This contradiction proves $N$ is free. Since this holds at every closed point, $M_{\rm reg}$ is a finite-rank vector bundle.

Localization sends each short exact sequence in $\mathcal O_c$ to a short exact sequence of vector bundles with connection by step 3.1 and local freeness from step 4.1. A short exact sequence of vector bundles is locally split, so its fiber sequence is exact. Parallel transport commutes with morphisms of connections; hence the fiber monodromy representations form a short exact sequence.

The $x$'s commute, and conjugation by $w$ sends the operator for $y$ to that for $wy$ because $c$ and the reflection forms are equivariant.

Write $T_y=\partial_y-\sum_s c_s\alpha_s(y)R_s$. The commutator $[T_y,T_z]$ is a differential-reflection operator on $\mathfrak h_{\rm reg}$, the complement of the reflection hyperplanes. By step 1.2 and Jacobi, $\operatorname{ad}_{[T_y,T_z]}(x)=[T_y,\kappa(z,x)]-[T_z,\kappa(y,x)]=[T_y,\kappa(z,x)]+[T_z,\kappa(x,y)]=0$, since $\kappa(y,z)=0$ for $y,z\in\mathfrak h$ and [F2] applies. The commutator with a group element uses the same formula as in [F1], by the $W$-covariance just checked.

In the crossed differential-operator algebra $\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})\rtimes W=\bigoplus_{w\in W}\mathcal D(\mathfrak h_{\rm reg})w$, the centralizer of all multiplication operators by $x\in\mathfrak h^*$ consists of multiplication by rational functions. Indeed, for a nonidentity $w$, choose $x$ with $wx\ne x$; the top differential-order term of $[D w,x]$ is the top term of $D$ multiplied by $wx-x$, so commutation forces $D=0$. For $w=1$, a differential operator commuting with every coordinate function has order zero, since the commutator of a positive-order operator with a coordinate has nonzero top symbol in some coordinate direction. Thus [T_y,T_z], which commutes with all $x$ by step 2.1, is multiplication by a rational function. Every $T_y$ kills $1$, so $[T_y,T_z]1=0$, and that multiplication function is zero. Hence the $T_y$ commute.

The assignments $x\mapsto m_x$, $w\mapsto w$, and $y\mapsto T_y$ now satisfy every relation in [F1]: the $x$'s commute, the $y$'s commute by step 3.1, the mixed commutator is step 1.2, and the $W$-action relation is the covariance in step 1.2. The quotient universal property therefore gives an $H_{1,c}$-module structure on $\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$.

The constant polynomial is killed by every $T_y$, and $W$ fixes it, so induction gives an $H_{1,c}$-module map $P_c=\Delta_c(\mathbf1)\to\mathbb C[\mathfrak h^*]$ sending $1\otimes1$ to $1$. It is surjective because multiplication by $\mathfrak h^*$ generates all polynomials. By PBW [F3], both spaces have the same monomial basis and this map is the identity on that basis, hence is an isomorphism. This is the asserted polynomial representation and action.

derivations.claim: Put all $x_i$ before every group symbol and all group symbols before all $y_j$, and order the $x_i$ and $y_j$ within their respective blocks by index. Use the defining relations as reductions: sort inverted pairs of $x$'s and of $y$'s; replace $w x$ by $w(x)w$; replace $y w$ by $w\,w^{-1}(y)$; replace $y x$ by $x y+\kappa(y,x)$; and multiply adjacent group symbols. Each vector in $w(x)$ or $w^{-1}(y)$ is expanded in the chosen finite bases. The irreducible words for these rules are precisely the displayed ordered monomials.

The reductions terminate. Order a word by the lexicographic measure consisting of (i) its number of $\mathfrak h$ and $\mathfrak h^*$ letters, (ii) its number of inversions relative to the declared normal order, and (iii) its number of group-symbol letters. A correction term $\kappa(y,x)$ strictly decreases (i); the main term $xy$ in the mixed reduction strictly decreases (ii); each group-crossing or same-side sorting rule strictly decreases (ii); and multiplication of adjacent group symbols preserves (i)–(ii) while decreasing (iii). Every reduction therefore decreases a well-founded measure on finite words, so no infinite reduction sequence exists.

All overlapping reductions have the following forms. Overlaps among two adjacent group multiplications or group-crossing rules agree because the action of $W$ is an action and group multiplication is associative. Overlaps among same-side sorting rules agree because the $x$'s commute with one another and the $y$'s commute with one another. A mixed group overlap $y w x$ agrees along its two reductions exactly by $W$-equivariance of $\kappa$ in [F2]. The only remaining overlaps are triples of vector letters, with two $y$'s and one $x$, or one $y$ and two $x$'s; the difference between reducing the two adjacent mixed pairs is the cyclic Jacobi expression from [F2], hence is zero. Reductions at disjoint pairs commute by substitution. Thus every one-step fork joins.

Termination from step 2.1 and the joining property from step 2.2 imply unique normal forms: by induction on the well-founded measure, if two first reductions differ, their join has smaller measure and therefore has the same normal form along both paths. Hence every word reduces uniquely to a linear combination of irreducible words. The reduction rules are consequences of [F1], so these words span the quotient. Conversely, the normal-form map annihilates each defining relation and all its left and right multiples; if a linear combination of irreducible words belonged to the defining ideal, its normal form would be both that combination and zero, so every coefficient would vanish. The irreducible words are therefore linearly independent in the quotient.

The irreducible words identified in step 1.1 are exactly $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}w y_1^{b_1}\cdots y_n^{b_n}$. Step 3.1 proves they form a basis. The tensor-product map in the Statement sends the tensor-product monomial basis to this basis, so it is an isomorphism. No restriction on $t$ or $c$ was used beyond the data definitions.

Since $y$ kills $E$, induction on polynomial degree shows that $y$ maps degree at most $d$ into degree at most $d-1$.

A product of $N$ elements of $\mathfrak h$ therefore maps every polynomial of degree at most $d$ to zero when $N>d$.
